articles.title: Hierarchy Emerges When Speed is Prioritized Over Quality in Group Decision-Making
articles.summary: Researchers from UC Merced have conducted computer simulations that challenge Robert Michels' iron law of oligarchy theory, which suggests that any organization eventually hands power to an elite.
articles.content: A century-old theory on democracy has been challenged by researchers from the University of California, Merced, who have found that not all groups inevitably drift towards rule by a few. According to Robert Michels' 1900s idea, also known as the iron law of oligarchy, any organization eventually hands power to an elite. However, recent models have supported this theory, suggesting that strong leaders facilitate agreement in large groups. New computer simulations conducted by researchers from UC Merced reveal a different outcome. The study found that hierarchy emerges when speed is prioritized, but not when quality takes precedence over speed. This indicates that the path towards oligarchy depends on how much time a group has to make decisions. The work was led by Chanuwas Aswamenakul, a graduate student and data scientist, in collaboration with professors Tyler Marghetis and Paul Smaldino from UC Merced's Department of Cognitive and Information Science. Smaldino is also an external professor at the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico. Smaldino and his team discovered that when groups prioritize quality over speed, they become more egalitarian rather than hierarchical. This suggests that the initial conditions and goals of a group play a crucial role in determining its future trajectory. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of how groups evolve over time. The researchers' results challenge the conventional wisdom that every organization will eventually succumb to rule by an elite, and instead highlight the importance of considering the specific circumstances under which groups develop. Groups in a virtual environment were simulated by the researchers to see how they made decisions and whether certain characteristics emerged as they evolved over time. Each group consisted of 500 members who held different opinions on what course of action was best, and consensus had to be reached before any decision could be implemented. The simulation involved giving rewards to groups that achieved their goals in a particular way. In one scenario, the reward went to groups that quickly came to an agreement, while in another scenario, it was given to those that deliberated more slowly, allowing for careful consideration of all viewpoints. This allowed the researchers to observe how different approaches affected group dynamics. When speed was the priority, a power imbalance emerged as a small number of influential individuals dominated many others. However, when slow and deliberate decision-making was rewarded, groups developed flatter structures where most members had relatively equal influence over outcomes. This pattern held true regardless of whether decisions were made through unanimous consent or majority vote. The researchers found that institutions can evolve to support careful deliberation, rather than necessarily being controlled by an elite few. In fact, this approach may be particularly beneficial in situations where time is not a constraint and correct results are valued over speed. Science itself appears to be an example of how slow and deliberate decision-making can prevail. Because the pursuit of knowledge values accuracy over expediency, scientific communities have generally resisted top-down control and instead allowed for more collaborative and inclusive approaches to research and discovery. In areas where resources are plentiful and decision-making can be a slow process, egalitarian institutions tend to flourish. This is according to a recent study that suggests the availability of resources plays a significant role in shaping the structure of decision-making groups. The researchers found that when resources are scarce and time is of the essence, leaders who can expedite consensus-building may become necessary. This could be why some cultures or subcultures prioritize speed over egalitarian norms, especially in situations where financial stability is not guaranteed. In conclusion, the study's findings suggest that the path to rule by the few is not inevitable when time is on the side of a group, and resources are abundant, allowing for more collaborative approaches to decision-making. articles.title: Restrictions on Public Gatherings Increase Across Africa
articles.summary: Opposition leaders across Africa are facing increasing pressure from authorities who are cracking down on their activities, with restrictions on public gatherings and legal action becoming common tactics used by governments to limit political freedoms.
articles.content: Opposition leaders across Africa are facing increasing pressure from authorities who are cracking down on their activities. Restrictions on public gatherings and legal action have become common tactics used by governments to limit political freedoms in countries such as Cameroon, Tanzania, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Zambia. The opposition argues that these measures are stifling democracy and preventing them from freely expressing their views to the public. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of Cameroon, highlighting the fear of arrest and violence that discourages political participation. In Cameroon, the law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Opposition figures in Africa are facing increasing pressure from governments as they try to mobilize support for their parties. In a separate development, police in Nigeria's Borno State arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing an anti-government slogan. The individuals were detained for alleged public disturbance and thuggery, rather than their political views. The men's arrest highlights the growing pressure faced by opposition voices in Africa. In some cases, even peaceful protests are met with force. The recent events in Nigeria demonstrate this trend. In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized the government for allegedly undermining democratic rights. He points to the closure of courts on August 24 as evidence of a retreat from democratic principles. The security operation that resulted in Mutotwe Kafwaya's death was allegedly carried out following intelligence on individuals deemed a threat to national security. Authorities claimed that officers came under fire and responded accordingly. This incident has added to growing concerns about the safety of opposition voices in Africa. Mundubile, who is facing treason and sedition charges alongside other opposition figures, has emphasized the need for fairness during his trial. He expressed hope for an open court process, stating "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us." This plea comes as Mundubile awaits the outcome of his case. Constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde and Cameroonian political analyst Kinang Derick Fai have both highlighted the challenges facing democratic development in Africa. articles.title: American Express Offers £10,000 Grants to 100 UK Small Businesses
articles.summary: The company is handing out £10,000 grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses through its partnership with Be the Business.
articles.content: American Express has announced a major initiative to support small business owners in the UK, providing them with a significant financial boost to help grow their ventures. The company is handing out £10,000 grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses through its partnership with Be the Business, a UK-based organisation that aims to enhance productivity among small enterprises. The move comes at a time when millions of people are turning away from traditional employment and opting for entrepreneurship as a means of building their own futures. To address this shift, American Express is investing £1 million in support for these individuals, providing them with the necessary resources to succeed. The grants will enable winners to revamp their premises, reach new customers, or introduce innovative initiatives that benefit their local communities. According to Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., even a modest investment can make a significant difference in the success of small businesses. This is reflected in the company's research findings, which suggest that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses have a positive impact on their local communities. Furthermore, two-thirds of respondents stated they would be more likely to shop with a business that employs people from the local area. The initiative is not only intended to support the growth of individual businesses but also to contribute to the development of vibrant and thriving destinations across the UK. By helping small businesses thrive, American Express hopes to foster active high streets and socially connected local communities. This goal is closely aligned with its research findings on consumer attitudes toward supporting local enterprises. The £10,000 grants are part of a larger scheme that requires winners to demonstrate how they spent the cash before receiving their full allocation. Five percent of each grant is held back until recipients provide evidence of their investment, underscoring American Express's commitment to transparency and accountability in its support for small business owners. To be eligible for this grant program, applicants must operate an independent, for-profit business that has been incorporated in the U.K. by December 1, 2025. In addition to being a registered company, businesses must also have at least one employee aside from owners or directors and cannot exceed 49 full-time equivalents in their workforce. A physical location is another requirement, as businesses must operate from a permanent premises that is open to customers in the U.K. Excluded from applying are online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and companies not registered with Companies House. The grant money can be used for specific projects such as upgrading equipment or digital marketing efforts but cannot cover everyday expenses like wages, rent, or stock. The grant is part of American Express's efforts to support British small business owners. With a growing number of entrepreneurs venturing into the market, this move aims to provide them with financial assistance. According to statistics, over 1.2 million startups have been established in the UK alone. In contrast, the US has a significant number of self-employed individuals, with more than 33 million Americans operating their own businesses. The majority of these small businesses operate without any employees, as reported by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Furthermore, around 82% of British startups are also single-employee operations. This trend is reflected in the growth of job titles on LinkedIn, where "founder" has seen a significant increase of 70% year-on-year, according to CEO Daniel Shapero. With access to resources and funding available, entrepreneurs can now focus on expanding their businesses and attracting more customers.
